audience.programmeDescription: Cognitive Science and Artificial Intelligence at Tilburg studies intelligence in humans and machines through computing, mathematics, neuroscience, language and philosophy. This example retains thirty credits for exchange study, followed by Hybrid Intelligence, Computational Linguistics, Ethics of AI and an empirical thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: UCR can combine AI with cognition, emphasise computational and autonomous systems, or focus on cognition and language with computational methods. The programmes share substantial computing and cognitive foundations. Tilburg has dedicated interface-design, agent-simulation, hybrid-AI and language-processing courses, alongside compulsory research projects and thesis. The relationships shown are partial.

componentNotes.y2-machine-learning: Entry requires Statistics for CSAI I and either Introduction to Programming or Data Structures and Algorithms.
componentNotes.y2-advanced-programming: Entry requires at least one of the earlier programming courses. Functional, concurrent and object-oriented programming build on those foundations.
componentNotes.y2-research: A group project covers the research cycle through an experiment or a machine-learning study. Entry requires Critical and Scientific Thinking, Statistics for CSAI I and ten hours in the human subject pool.
componentNotes.y3-exchange: Thirty credits are reserved for approved study at a partner university. The destination and courses remain open. The package must meet entry, academic quality, coherence and non-overlap requirements.
componentNotes.y3-thesis: The twelve-credit thesis is a supervised empirical quantitative study in cognitive science and artificial intelligence, including programming, analysis and academic reporting. Entry requires all first-year courses and at least sixty later-year credits. It cannot start before semester six.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

BENGATE102.name: Research Methods & Statistics
BENGATE102.text: Research Methods & Statistics introduces research design, operationalisation, measurement, sampling, surveys and experiments. Students study descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression using R and R Commander. A group project develops a research plan and instruments, collects and analyses data, and reports findings under research-ethics and privacy requirements.

DISARIN111.name: AI Ethics
DISARIN111.text: AI Ethics examines artificial intelligence from philosophical and psychological perspectives. Topics include fairness, privacy, responsibility, human-value alignment, moral status and political or existential risks. Students apply ethical frameworks to questions about human behaviour and interaction, synthesise research in an analytical psychology project, and produce a research-based podcast.

DISARIN211.name: Decision-making in AI
DISARIN211.text: Decision-making in AI examines how intelligent agents make decisions under uncertainty. Students study probability, Bayesian networks, temporal models, expected utility, Markov decision processes, partial observability and bandit problems. Multi-agent decisions and probabilistic programming extend the analysis, supported by equations, numerical examples and scientific papers.

Students work with propositions, quantified statements, sets, Boolean algebra, functions and relations, direct and indirect proofs, induction and recursion. A final component models processes and games without chance and investigates winning strategies.

HCBCOGN312.name: Psycholinguistics
HCBCOGN312.text: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.
